title: Starburst Cluster Shows Celestial Fireworks
caption: Star cluster NGC 3603 and its nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 3603 · constellation Carina · about 20,000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A bright, yellow-white cluster of young stars bursts out like an aerial firework above wisps of glowing purple gas. The cluster, NGC 3603, sits at the heart of a nebula 20,000 light-years away in the constellation Carina, and the clouds of gas and dust around it are raw material for new stars.

The scene is less peaceful than it looks, since violent stellar winds and ultraviolet radiation have blown an enormous cavity in the surrounding gas and dust, which leaves the cluster in plain view. Most of its stars were born at roughly one time, yet they vary in size, mass, temperature and color. Because a star's mass sets the course of its life, a cluster like this holds stars at many stages.
Among its members are some of the most massive stars known. Such stars burn through their hydrogen quickly and end their lives as supernovae.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light that traces sulfur, hydrogen and iron. F164N ([Fe II]) is shown in red, F128N (Paschen-beta) in yellow, F673N ([S II]) in green, F656N (H-alpha) in blue and F555W in white.
understand.eye: Part of the light is infrared, invisible to the eye, and narrow filters isolate the glow of individual elements, so the colors do not match what an eye would see.

explore: Clusters like NGC 3603 offer clues to how massive stars formed in the early, distant universe. Being relatively close, it is also a useful lab for the bursts of star formation set off when galaxies collide.
